title: The five ways
hook: Aquinas offers five paths from the world to God, like motion needing a first mover

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abelard and Heloise: yes and no side by side, and an abbess with hard questions. Your line was by doubting we come to inquiry. Who did you ask about your question? Day one thousand two hundred fifty.

A kettle sits on a stove. The water in it is cold, but it could be hot. Turn on the flame, and the heat that's really in the fire passes into the water, and the water starts to move. Bubbles. Steam. A whistle. Nothing about that is mysterious. But a Dominican friar named Thomas Aquinas looked at moments exactly this ordinary, and asked where the chain of them leads. His answer opens with a plain sentence: the existence of God can be proved in five ways. And the first way starts with something moving.

For Aquinas, motion means any change at all: something that could be one way becoming that way. His own example is fire making wood hot. The wood can be hot; the fire actually is hot; so the fire moves the wood. Here's the rule he draws from it: whatever is moved is moved by another. The wood by the fire, the fire by something else, all at once, like a hand moving a stick that moves a stone. That chain can't go on to infinity, he argues, or there would be no first mover, and so no other mover either. So there must be a first mover, moved by nothing, and this, he says, everyone understands to be God. That's the first way. The other four follow the same shape. Causes, which need a first cause. Things that come and go, which need something that doesn't come and go. Things that are more or less good and true, which point to what is best and truest. And things without minds that still act toward a goal, like an arrow flying straight because an archer aimed it. Two more details. First, Aquinas starts from the world, not from an idea in the mind. He wasn't persuaded that God's existence is obvious to us just from the definition. Second, he never says the five ways tell us everything. They show that God is, not what God is. Some truths about God, he says, reason can't reach without God revealing them. Paul wrote that God's invisible things are "clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made." Aquinas took him at his word, and started with a moving world.
screen: `THAT GOD IS, NOT WHAT GOD IS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at motion and wonder. Settle, and breathe. Find something moving: a curtain in a draft, leaves outside, steam from a cup, your own chest rising. Watch it. Then ask what moves it. The air. And what moves the air? Follow the chain back a few links, gently, without needing an answer. Let your wonder go as far as it wants. If you pray, you can thank God for one thing you watched move. The bell holds the time.
The five ways. Aquinas's five paths from the world to God, starting with motion: whatever is moved is moved by another, back to a first mover.
Your line: everything moves. Today, when you see something change, water boiling, a light turning green, ask once what set it moving. Day one thousand two hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Catholic schools and seminaries teach Aquinas's five ways as part of philosophy, and Christians of other churches meet them in theology and apologetics classes, where they are still debated.

notes: Aquinas is paraphrased (the 1920 English Dominican translation is not on the validator's list). Check: 'the existence of God can be proved in five ways' (I q.2 a.3); motion as reduction from potentiality to actuality, with fire and wood; 'whatever is moved is moved by another'; no infinite regress; 'and this everyone understands to be God'; the arrow and the archer (fifth way).
'He wasn't persuaded that God's existence is obvious to us just from the definition' refers to I q.2 a.1, where Aquinas answers an Anselm-style argument; the script does not name Anselm. Confirm.

'They show that God is, not what God is': Aquinas says we cannot know what God is, only what God is not (I q.3 prologue); confirm the paraphrase. 'For the rest, he turns to scripture' simplifies I q.1 a.1; confirm.

Editor pass: cut the stock line 'two things are easy to miss'; replaced 'for the rest, he turns to scripture' (an oversimplification) with Aquinas's point in I q.1 a.1 that some truths about God need revelation, in the teach and in the myth reveal.
Hook's kettle is a modern illustration of Aquinas's own fire-and-wood example; the 'Dominican friar' description is standard.
Original: quinque viae; pronunciation given in classical-leaning style.

Audit (2026-10-02): the first way was framed as a chain running backward in time (fork: 'fire, the one who lit it'); Aquinas's argument concerns movers acting together now, and he holds elsewhere that reason alone cannot rule out an endless past series (I q.46 a.2 ad 7). Teach and fork now use his own wording (no infinite series, else no first mover and so no other mover) and his hand-stick-stone picture (ST I q.2 a.3; cf. Summa contra Gentiles 1.13); confirm. Original pronunciation made consistently ecclesiastical.
